# I. Resource & Material Base → Distribution & Logistics → Allocation Mechanisms

## Design Proposal: Priority Classes, a Ration Ladder, and Points for the Ordinary Economy

---

## 0. Where this branch sits in the inherited set

Node I.1 and branches I.2.1–I.2.2 have already decided *how most allocation
happens* — this branch designs what remains. The inherited allocation layer:

|Flow / capacity|Allocation already decided|Source|
|---|---|---|
| Water | Non-market hierarchy: env. flows > domestic > essential > ag > industrial > non-essential; staged drought protocol (150 L/p/d cap at Stage 3, 50 L/p/d Stage 4) | Water log |
| Energy | No financial markets; PPAs/tolling; lifeline rate 200 kWh/mo discounted | Energy log |
| Food staple calories | Tiered self-sufficiency + inter-regional grain band, firm delivery obligations; buffer-stock-backed | Food log, DEC-001 |
| Spine track capacity | Booked, grain band + ammonia first | DEC-007 |
| Node storage capacity | Booked by class, one stock ledger | DEC-011 |
| Critical minerals | Stockpiles + bilateral agreements, no futures | Materials log |

**What is genuinely undecided:** (1) the **priority order among claimants** when
a scarce good (fuel, spare parts, material lots) must be curtailed — the
RTA×REA-type curtailment rows in the arbitration spec assume a priority scale
that no log yet defines; (2) the **food ration ladder thresholds** — the water
log has a four-stage ladder with numbers, food has none; (3) the **allocation
of ordinary consumer goods (Class C)** — everything behind the booked/critical
layer has no designed mechanism; (4) **who runs ration administration** once a
ladder activates.

**Arithmetic done first (from cited sources):** the food ration ladder's
calibration. The balance sheet uses ~1,400 kcal/cap/day as the staple-calorie
baseline; the Sphere/WFP emergency standard is 2,100 kcal/p/day total. The
6-week Class B grain buffer for a 2M-person region (25–29 kt) stretches to
**~900 kcal/cap/day of staple grain at full drawdown** (25,000 t × 3,100
kcal/kg ÷ 2M people ÷ 42 days) — under half the emergency standard — so the
ladder must assume buffer + continued local water-thin production + band
resumption together, never the buffer alone. Buffer alone is a bridge, not a
diet.

## 1. Decision 1 — Four priority classes for curtailable scarce inputs (firm)

**The decision:** every scarce curtailable input (e-fuel, spare parts, material
lots, dispatchable electricity shares beyond the PPA base) carries a published
**priority class** that binds all curtailment decisions in the node:

- **P1 — Life-support:** hospitals, water treatment, sanitation continuity.
  Never curtailed below lifeline levels (water 150 L/p/d Stage-3 equivalence;
  energy lifeline rate; treatment-chemical flow).
- **P2 — Critical infrastructure operations:** grid black-start and reserve
  margin, spine operations, firefighting, ammonia plants' protected
  agricultural floor (arbitration spec §2.5 lifeline-fertilizer requirement —
  now given its class), buffer-stock rotation itself.
- **P3 — Food-chain operations:** harvest machinery, food processing and cold
  chain, grain-band origination and warehousing.
- **P4 — Everything else,** including discretionary freight, industry outside
  the materials log's production floors, and non-critical commerce.

**Mechanism and actor:** each consigning authority publishes the priority class
with its goods in the classification register (storage log, Decision 1) — one
register, two numbers per good (class, priority). Curtailment decisions follow
the class order **without discretionary reordering**; within a class,
pro-rata by booked volume — no case-by-case ranking. The arbitration spec's
requirement 2 (dispute resolution faster than the fastest physical trigger)
applies: a P1 shortfall claim is resolved in hours, not committee cycles.

**Rationale:** the arbitration spec's RTA×REA row (§2.9) requires "a protected
ammonia slot pair" and §2.8 requires protected agro-machinery share — both are
case-specific instances of what is here generalized to one priority scale.
Real-world comparison: the EU's 2022 gas-demand reduction regulation (Council Regulation (EU) 2022/1854) used protected-consumer classes exactly this way —
hospitals and households protected, industry curtailed by schedule — and the
mechanism worked top-down because the classes were pre-agreed, not negotiated
during the crisis.

**Trade-off (named):** fixed priority classes are coarse — a P3 food-chain
claim that is genuinely life-supporting (remote-region harvest during a
failure window) cannot leapfrog P2 without an exception event, adding
latency. The rejected alternative — case-by-case emergency boards deciding
each curtailment — was rejected because case-by-case ranking under time
pressure is exactly where capture and favoritism enter (the water log removed
discretionary triggers from drought response for the same reason).

**Scale:** regional, inter-regional for band flows. **Status: firm** (the
class content of specific goods follows the register, tentative per-good).

## 2. Decision 2 — Food and goods ration ladder with pre-numeric triggers (firm)

**The decision:** goods scarcity inherits the water log's staged-trigger
architecture — pre-numeric thresholds, automatic activation, no discretionary
lag:

- **R0 (normal):** booked flows + Class C allocation (Decision 3).
- **R1 (buffer drawdown begins):** band flow delayed >2 weeks or buffer
  drawdown started: RTA activates buffer rotation into consumption; booked-slot
  redirection per the storage log's protocol. Drawdown rate at R1: normal
  rotation pace (stock circulates into consumption, not emergency drawdown).
- **R2 (buffer half-empty, calendar backstop >4 wk):** cumulative drawdown
  reaches **50% of Class B stock**, or interruption age exceeds 4 weeks —
  whichever fires first: universal staples ration at **1,400
  kcal/cap/day staple-basket floor** (the balance sheet's staple baseline —
  the floor is set where the tiered arid self-sufficiency target already
  guarantees local supply) + continued Class F fresh distribution. Drawdown
  rate steps up at R2.
- **R3 (freeboard <2 weeks, calendar backstop >8 wk):** remaining Class B
  freeboard falls below **2 weeks of staple flow**, or interruption age exceeds
  8 weeks — whichever fires first: full emergency ration **2,100 kcal/cap/day
  total** (Sphere/WFP standard) with ~2 weeks of buffer remaining under the
  trigger and inter-regional famine-commons activation as R3's sustenance
  continuation. Drawdown rate at R3: full stretch (~900 kcal staple
  contribution), the remaining freeboard carrying the ladder to the famine-
  commons handover at ~wk 6–8 of stock age.

**Mechanism and actor:** the RTA executes goods-side logistics; the RFA holds
famine-protocol authority (its mandate); the jointly-signed response
protocol from the storage log (§4 there) defines who fires what. Rationing
authorization is pre-delegated — the same instrument the storage log parked
pending Domain IV recognition; this decision binds the *food thresholds* to
that instrument.

**Rationale:** the water log's drought protocol exists because pre-defined
triggers eliminate political indecision lag (Cape Town Day Zero); food
scarcity has the same lag pathology with a faster death toll. The thresholds
are tied to numbers already in the node (1,400 staple baseline; 2,100 Sphere
standard) so the ladder cannot be gamed by redefinition.

**Trade-off (named):** R2's 1,400 kcal staple floor is deliberately *not* the
full 2,100 — a region activates full emergency ration only when scarcity is
real, which saves the difference during short interruptions but accepts that
R2 stretches people below comfort (real-world comparison: UK WWII first-stage
rationing cut conveniences, not calories; full-calorie rationing arrived only
when supply actually failed). The rejected alternative — single-threshold
full-ration — overtriggers, wasting buffer rotation on R1-scale events and
falsely signaling famine frequency.

**Scale:** regional activation, inter-regional famine-commons coordination at
R3. **Status: firm** (thresholds tied to logged numbers; the R3 famine-commons
mechanism itself is Domain II's to design — flagged below).

## 3. Decision 3 — Class C (ordinary) goods: fixed-price retail with points rationing, no price rationing (firm)

**The decision:** ordinary consumer goods allocate through **fixed-price
retail channels; when a Class C good is scarce, allocation converts to
non-transferable household points rationing, not price escalation.** Points
are per-capita weekly allotments by category (e.g. clothing points, durables
points), consolidateable within a household, non-transferable between
households, expiring at period end — no points market, no resale.

**Mechanism and actor:** retail allocation is Domain II's market design for
the non-critical economy; this branch fixes only the **ration-conversion
trigger and the points architecture** because rationing is a logistics
function (inventory visibility, WMS integration, redemption auditing) the RTA
already owns. Points redemption runs through the same WMS stock ledger — the
inventory surface and the ration surface are one system, no separate
ration-card bureaucracy. Administration sits with the RTA; appeals go through
the consigning authorities' existing client channels; enforcement (black
markets, fraud) is Domain IV's.

**Numbers:** point allotment sizing is proportional to buffer-checked supply
(published quarterly per the storage log); the design target is that points
bind for **<20% of Class C categories in a normal year** — rationing is a
contingency layer, not the operating system of the ordinary economy.

**Rationale:** price rationing on scarce necessities allocates by willingness-
to-pay, which concentrates social breakdown pressure exactly when the society
is least able to absorb it (real-world comparison: the UK's WWII points
system vs. free price escalation — points covered clothing and durables;
unrationed staple prices stayed contained because staples were outright
rationed
staples were outright rationed; Cuba's *libreta* persists because the
transferable-points alternative produced black markets in every society that
tried one). Fixed prices + points keep the market's convenience function
without letting it become the scarcity allocator — consistent with the
node's established no-market lineage, now extended to the demand side rather
than only supply-side infrastructure.

**Trade-off (named):** non-transferable points kill the informal-exchange
mechanism through which household heterogeneity is normally smoothed (a
childless household cannot sell clothing points to a household with children)
— genuine deadweight loss, accepted because the transferable version
systematically produced black markets in every historical deployment
(WWII UK, Soviet second economy). The rejected alternative — market pricing
plus universal transfer sufficient to keep necessities purchasable — depends
on a currency/redistribution design Domain II has not yet built, and would
make goods allocation hostage to cash-transfer infrastructure functioning
during exactly the crises where that infrastructure is under stress.

**Scale:** regional retail; points architecture regional, household-scale in
use. **Status: firm** (category list and 20% target tentative, reviewed
annually with the stock ledger).

## 4. Decision 4 — Ration administration is an RTA logistics function with civil-claims enforcement (tentative)

**The decision:** once a ladder stage activates, **administration runs
through the RTA's existing machinery** (WMS ledger, booked slots, custody,
audit) — no new ration authority is created; the *legal* enforcement of
redemption rights and fraud cases is Domain IV's, and ration-appeal rights
are civil claims appealable through the consigning authorities' existing
client channels under the arbitration spec's transition rule (any
inter-authority agreement must be loggable against the §2 collision table).

**Mechanism and actor:** the RTA publishes the activated ladder's per-stage
redemption rules through the same quarterly-publication pipeline; redemption
receipts are civil documents; the RTA audits redemption distribution
annually with the rotation audit. This is deliberately an adaptation of an
existing authority, not a fifth+ creation — the integration review's
authority-accumulation warning (spec §4, "don't repeat the tripartite
template") prices new authority creation as the project's costliest move; this
branch adds zero collision rows beyond the RTA pairs already in spec
§2.8–2.10.

**Rationale:** storage log Decision 4 already pre-delegated ration
authorization to the RTA/consigning-branch protocol; the administrator needs
no new powers, only equipment (ledger, custody, audit) it already holds. A
separate ration authority would duplicate the WMS, fork the stock ledger,
and add a tenth collision row to an arbitration problem Domain III has not
even begun to solve (spec §2.1–2.10).

**Trade-off (named):** civil-claims-based enforcement is slower than an
administrative tribunal in fraud cases — genuine enforcement lag, accepted
because administrative-tribunal speed in a rationing regime historically
converts into arbitrary local power (real-world comparison: wartime ration
boards' local discretion was the largest single corruption surface in most
examined regimes). The rejected alternative — a dedicated ration tribunal —
was rejected on authority-accumulation grounds; revisit if Domain IV's
civil-process latency exceeds the fraud-relevant decision window.

**Scale:** regional. **Status: tentative — must fit Domain III's arbitration
mechanism (nine RTA×consignor collision rows already exist) and Domain IV's
civil-process design; both confirm before firming, per the storage log's
pre-delegation pattern.**

## 6. Vision-Essay Alignment Notes

- **Pre-numeric triggers as anti-decay architecture:** both Decision 1's class
  ordering and Decision 2's ladder remove discretionary ranking from crisis
  moments — the water log's drought-protocol logic applied to goods; the
  essay's decay mechanism is countered by making activation arithmetic, not
  judgment.
- **Non-transferable points:** the design accepts deadweight loss to prevent
  the black-market dynamic that historically turned ration currencies into
  shadow money — a named efficiency sacrifice of exactly the kind the
  essay's persistence-over-optimization principle asks for.
- **No new authority:** Decision 4 reuses the RTA's logistics machinery
  instead of creating a ration authority — the integration review's
  authority-accumulation warning prices new-authority creation as costliest;
  the branch adds zero collision rows beyond the RTA pairs already in spec
  §2.8–2.10.
- **Fixed prices over price signals for necessities:** extends the node's
  no-market lineage to the demand side; the essay doesn't prescribe market
  vs. non-market allocation, and the justification here is the same one the
  water log used — market allocation optimizes for highest-value use, the
  wrong allocator under life-supporting scarcity.

## 1. Internal Contradiction Sweep

Four contradictions found. Contradictions A and B are **arithmetic**, not
conceptual — they are the exact failure mode the skill's verification loop
warns about, and they should be settled numerically, not rhetorically.

**Contradiction A: The spine test (≥1.5 Mt/yr) vs. the arid region's own flow arithmetic**
Transport Decision 2 (Transport log, spine designation) admits a corridor to
spine status only at ≥1.5 Mt/yr forecast load, and its own §0/§2 text arithmetically
sizes the arid region's flows: grain band 0.22–0.25 Mt/yr (DEC-001; balance
sheet §1.1), own-food ammonia ~13 kt/yr (balance sheet §1.3, 5–8 kg N/cap/yr
× 2M), steel/components 0.4–0.6 Mt/yr (Materials log, 200–300 kg/cap/yr × 2M,
of which an unknown share is intra-regional). Even generously double-counting,
the named node flows on an arid corridor sum to **≲0.7–1.1 Mt/yr** — below the
spine threshold. Decision 2 then states the *opposite* branch behavior for
exactly this case: "arid regions without a qualifying spine corridor get spine
build-out priority under Decision 2's ≥1.5 Mt/yr test." A corridor cannot
simultaneously fail a 1.5 Mt/yr test and qualify for spine priority by that
test. If arid corridors are not spines, they get no double-stack electrified
freight or catenary build-out, and the modal hierarchy's remaining options are
waterborne (geography-dependent) or e-fuel road exceptions — which the
Decision 3 line ("never to road/rail") and the 400–1,200 kWh/cap/yr band both
constrain. **Verdict: an unresolved threshold-vs-volume inconsistency inside one
branch, with node-level consequences** (buffer siting in I.2.2 assumes spine
nodes; I.2.3's booked-slot redirection assumes booked capacity exists).

**Contradiction B: The ration ladder's R3 trigger fires after the buffer is exhausted**
The buffer is six weeks of flow (Transport log, DEC-009; Storage log §0:
25–29 kt ≈ 5.2–6.9 weeks of the arid grain flow). Storage Decision 1 makes
that six-week stock Class B policy, and Allocation Decision 2 calibrates the
ladder from it. But the ladder's triggers run on interruption *age* — R1 fires
at band delay >2 weeks, R2 at >4 weeks, R3 at >8 weeks "with the buffer at
full stretch (~900 kcal/cap/day staple contribution)." At full stretch
(900 kcal/cap/day × 42 days — the Allocation log's own arithmetic), the buffer
is fully consumed by roughly week 6. R3 at week 8 — the stage that most
depends on buffer sustenance — arrives to an **empty buffer**. R2's 1,400
kcal/cap/day floor assumes buffer rotation + local water-thin production +
band resumption together (Allocation §0 says exactly this), so the gap closes
only under a favorable resumption case; the unfavorable case — what R3 exists
for — is precisely the one the arithmetic leaves uncovered for weeks 6–8+.
This is a timing-sequence contradiction between Storage Decision 1/2 and
Allocation Decision 2, not a disagreement about buffer size. **Verdict:
unresolved; the R-ladder's trigger ages and the buffer's runway need a joint
recompute in one work package** (candidates the fixer may consider, not decided
here: graded drawdown rates by stage, trigger ages measured from buffer
drawdown start rather than interruption start, or a re-derived R3 with a
non-buffer famine-commons assumption).

**Contradiction C: Two parallel curtailment ladders with no crosswalk**
The node now contains two published scarcity-ordering schemes: the water log's
allocation hierarchy + staged drought protocol (env. flows > domestic >
essential > ag > industrial > non-essential; Stage 3 cap 150 L/p/d, Stage 4
50 L/p/d), and Allocation Decision 1's P1–P4 priority classes (life-support >
critical infrastructure > food-chain > everything else). Several claimants
appear in both (industrial, agriculture, treatment chemicals) at different
positions: agriculture sits *below* domestic in the water ladder but
*above* discretionary commerce in the P-ladder; industrial sits P4 on goods
but above non-essential on water. No log defines which ladder governs when
water scarcity and goods scarcity co-occur, and the water log's ag position and
the P-ladder's P3 position imply different priorities for the same harvest.
Additionally, e-fuels carry their own published allocation order (Transport
Decision 3: aviation first, shipping second, surplus to machinery) — a third
ordering that is not listed in the classification register's priority column
(Allocation Decision 1 says the register carries "one register, two numbers
per good: class, priority" — e-fuel's air-first priority order is not a
P-class and is left unreconciled). The storage log deploys exactly this pattern
the right way: its Decision 4 protocol template inherits the water log's
drought triggers *verbatim*. **Verdict: unresolved; needs one cross-work
addition** — a ladder crosswalk (water stage × P-class × e-fuel order) in the
register design, plus an e-fuel priority class in the register. Diagnose
first; who writes it (allocation vs. water work package) is an ownership
decision to make at fix time.

**Contradiction D: Pro-rata-by-booked-volume is undefined for most P3/P4 claimants**
Allocation Decision 1 allocates within a priority class "pro-rata by booked
volume." Booked volume is a defined concept exactly where DEC-007/DEC-011
created bookings: spine train paths and node storage. P4 explicitly includes
discretionary freight, non-critical commerce, and P3 includes food-chain
operations spread across non-spine corridors, last-mile drayage, Class F
settlement-hub flows — none of which book anything in the current design
(I.2.1 non-spine corridors "carry regional redistribution and last-mile
traffic only" with no specified booking). Pro-rata-by-booked-volume is thus
undefined at exactly the claim classes it most affects. **Verdict: narrow but
real; a small allocation work package must choose between extending booking
downward, a fallback (e.g. consumption-share) rule for unbooked claimants, or
a second pro-rata basis.**

## 2. Scale Coherence Within the Node

This node is **more scale-coherent than I.1 was at its integration**. All
three branches operate on the RTA's regional scale, use the same corridor
geography, and inherit each other's mechanisms end-to-end (booked spine slots
→ stocked at spine nodes → ration redirection through the same slots). The
scale map entries line up: settlement (Class F hubs, points redemption) /
regional (RTA, register, ledger, ladder) / inter-regional (spines, band,
famine commons).

Two seams remain:

- **The inter-regional layer has no governing instrument.** Transport's scale
  map says explicitly: "no global transport authority; corridor agreements
  between RTAs only." But three node-critical mechanisms are inter-regional in
  a way a bilateral corridor agreement cannot cover: spine continuity across
  two RTAs' jurisdictions, dual-origin qualification where one region's RFA
  certifies while another's RTA credentials (Storage Decision 3), and R3
  famine-commons activation spanning multiple regions simultaneously
  (Allocation Decision 2). The arbitration spec (accepted as the node's
  boundary-logics artifact) contains pairwise RTA↔RFA/REA/WA rows (§2.8–2.10)
  but **no RTA↔RTA row** — the spec was written when the RTA was one region's
  authority; the moment it became a *class* of peer authorities with joint
  obligations, its own collisions became possible (competing spine bookings on
  a shared corridor, disagreements on origin qualification, famine-commons
  activation asymmetry). Diagnosed here as a spec-gap finding; fixing it (a
  collision-table row or a named inter-regional instrument) is a small
  design decision for a work package.
- **Passenger transport ownership is a node-level omission, not a parked
  detail.** I.2.1 parks it "belongs to this node's future work or Domain
  VIII." That deferral consumes the RTA's whole institutional shape (boards,
  fees, staffing of 40–80/region) for freight only, then leaves the node
  called simply "Distribution & Logistics" while passenger mobility — the
  larger electricity- and infrastructure-consumer by trip-count — is
  unowned somewhere else. This is best re-parked **at the node level with an
  explicit ownership arrow** (whether it becomes I.2.x or belongs to Domain
  VIII's "physical infrastructure" is a work-package decision), because any
  future passenger-electrification arithmetic will draw on the same 400–1,200
  kWh/cap/yr band this node already claims.

The chain Transport → Storage → Allocation is deliberately linear and
door-to-door in form: I.2.1 creates booked slots and buffer custody (DEC-009),

builds the scarcity logic on both (priorities, ladder, points, DEC-014/015).
That chain is audited and holds at the mechanism level. Specific results:

**Dep. 1: Allocation → Storage (register + WMS) — VERIFIED.** I.2.3's Decision 1
and 3 both run through I.2.2's classification register and WMS stock ledger;
the storage log grants that surface (Decision 2's one open-source WMS,
cross-publishing per arbitration-spec requirement 3). No assumed input.

**Dep. 2: Storage → Transport (spine nodes, booked slots) — VERIFIED but dependent on Contradiction A.** The mechanism is fully specified (I.2.2's §0
precedent list, Decision 2's "booked like track") — but it presumes spine
nodes exist, which is exactly what Contradiction A leaves dangling for arid
regions. This is the node's clearest case of one branch's verified dependency
sitting on another branch's unresolved number.

**Dep. 3: Buffer quantities for non-food/non-ammonia goods — assumed inputs from upstream branches.** Storage §0's table estimates water-treatment chemicals
(1–2 kg/cap/yr) and medicines (0.5–2 kg/cap/yr) as *est.*, sourced to no
logged branch decision. Water log has no treatment-chemical flow line; Health

rule) will demand **logged two-number classifications** from somewhere —
currently no branch is logged as the consigning authority for these goods,
and the register's closure rule will not let them be quietly added under
RTA's discretion. **Verdict: dependents exist with no upstream quantity owner
— flagged, small.**

**Dep. 4: Cold-chain Class F resilience under compound scarcity — unexamined.**
Storage Decision 1 states Class F's resilience comes "from redundant flow, not
stock." Under the node's own compound-scarcity configuration (water Stage 3 +
P2 grid curtailment + R2 rationing firing together — Adversarial but
arithmetically reachable, e.g. a hot drought simultaneous with a band
interruption), Class F perishables fail in days while Class B staples hold.
The ladder covers staple calories at R2/R3 but has **no Class F provisioning
line** — protein/fresh produce gaps during multi-week events are unaccounted.
I.1's nutrition floor (food log's 2,100 kcal, Sphere standard) counts
calories, not composition. **Verdict: real gap; belongs to a food+storage
joint work package, not an integration-session fix.**

**Dep. 5: Buffer quantities per consigning branch ride I.1's own stockpile

siting, and I.2.3's points WMS share this wait. It is *consistently logged*

### DEC-001 — Arid-region water allocation vs. food self-sufficiency

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, Node I.1 integration session (Blocker 1).
**Scope:** [Resource & Material Base → Water & Sanitation] × [Food/Agriculture];
Contradiction A.

**Question:** How should the water-food trade-off be resolved in arid and
semi-arid regions?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-001-alt-A — Flow floor inviolable, self-sufficiency tiered by water
  scarcity [CHOSEN]:** Keep the ≥50% environmental flow floor absolutely firm.
  Water-self-sufficiency in food is redefined as a sliding scale: arid regions
  target 70% only for water-thin crops (olives, lupins, dryland grains), drop to
  30–40% for water-thick staples, and are explicitly specced as import-reliant for
  those — a designed inter-regional "virtual water" flows architecture, not market
  chance. Trade-off named: arid settlements accept permanent caloric dependency on
  wet-region trade partners, concentrating a new vulnerability into Domain II's
  trade design.
- **DEC-001-alt-B — Caloric target holds everywhere, water architecture scales up
  instead [NOT CHOSEN]:** Keep 70% self-sufficiency firm in all regions. Arid
  regions meet it by restructuring the food system: expanded desalination + inland
  conveyance, high-value-per-drop cropping (nuts, greenhouse, protected
  agriculture), dietary shifts toward low-water-weight foods, heavy
  irrigation-drainage reuse. Flow floor stays 50% but the extractable pie grows via
  desal and treated-wastewater reuse. Trade-off: enormous capital and energy cost
  (ties to energy log), inland desal brine disposal is a real ecological problem,
  and in the most extreme regions no water architecture can close the gap —
  population sizing would have to give, which nobody has proposed.
- **DEC-001-alt-C — Flow floor becomes a two-tier regime: 40% degraded / 50%
  restored [NOT CHOSEN]:** Soften the water log: 50% floor in currently-functioning
  watersheds, 40% minimum in degraded watersheds under active 30-year restoration
  schedules, freeing more extractable water for arid agriculture to hit 70% more
  often. Trade-off: weakens the firmest decision in the water log and sets a
  precedent that firm decisions bend under pressure — a risk to the whole
  integrity-of-precedent system the other logs lean on.
- **DEC-001-alt-D — Rethink the target itself: nutrition-complete, not
  calorie-complete [NOT CHOSEN]:** Replace "70% caloric self-sufficiency" with a
  nutritionally-complete target: each region supplies its own protein, fats, and
  micronutrients from water-cheap production (arid: legumes, oil crops, small
  ruminants, dates), while water-thick calories (bread grains, rice, sugar) always
  flow through a protected inter-regional grain commons with firm delivery
  obligations. Trade-off: requires a novel institutional layer inside the food
  branch, and the 70%/calories number was partly chosen because it is easy to
  stress-test and communicate.

**Decision:** alt-A. Environmental flow floor declared inviolable in all watersheds;
the food branch's 70% caloric self-sufficiency target amended to tier by water
availability (arid: 70% for water-thin production, 30–40% for water-thick staples;
residual via a designed inter-regional grain flows band with firm delivery
obligations). Slogan recorded: "food targets bend, not rivers."

**Rationale:** ecological integrity of rivers/aquifers is effectively irreversible
once destroyed; food is substitutable across space. Making the dependency explicit
and institutionally designed beats both failed self-sufficiency (silent famine
risk) and market dependence (the contested Domain II free-trade assumption).

**Trade-offs accepted:** permanent caloric dependency of arid regions on wet-region
partners; new vulnerability concentrated in Domain II's grain-band design.

**Propagations:** Domain II (grain-band exchange mechanics — bilateral treaty vs.
pooled commons unresolved); Domain VIII (arid settlement sizing); Domain X (flow
floor as genuinely inviolable norm). Downstream confirmation: Blocker 2's balance
sheet later showed the physical water residual (~505–540 m³/cap/yr) supports only
~27–29% of staple calories from water-thick crops — alt-B was arithmetically
unavailable; the tiered targets were physically forced, not merely preferred.

### DEC-002 — Joint resource balance sheet: framing precedent

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, Node I.1 integration session (Blocker 2).
**Scope:** all four branches of Node I.1; new artifact 01-1-resource-balance-sheet.md.

**Question:** When budgets conflict (land, water, energy, labor), what should the
joint resource balance sheet treat as the fixed constraint and what as the flexing
variable?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-002-alt-A — Population-first: population is the output, budget is the
  constraint [CHOSEN]:** Fix the environmental flow floor, water allocation,
  100–150 L/p/d, and material/labor throughput as hard constraints; then compute
  what arid-region settlement population is actually supportable. Trade-off:
  treats settlement size as a design output and forces some regions to shrink or
  stabilize, which no branch has proposed yet.
- **DEC-002-alt-B — Consumption-first: consumption targets are hard, land/labor
  flex to meet them [NOT CHOSEN]:** Fix 70% self-sufficiency in non-arid regions,
  4,000–6,000 kWh/cap/yr, 100–150 L/p/d as commitments to meet regardless.
  Trade-off: tends to expand extractive footprint to chase consumption numbers,
  which is the exact monoculture/optimization failure mode the essay warns against.
- **DEC-002-alt-C — Sliding-scale: both population and consumption flex, one fixed
  quality-of-life floor [NOT CHOSEN]:** Fix only a minimal floor (e.g. WHO
  50 L/p/d water, 2,200 kcal/day food, 2,000 kWh/cap/yr electricity) and let both
  population and consumption adjust toward it. Trade-off: introduces a non-binding
  upper bound and makes the "materially good life" target mushy — risks losing the
  design discipline the per-branch numbers were chosen to impose.

**Decision:** alt-A. Population is the output variable; water/land/energy/labor
budgets are the constraints.

**Rationale:** matches what water-stressed basins actually face (Colorado River,
Murray–Darling); population/sizing is the adaptable variable, not the target.

**Trade-offs accepted:** settlement sizing becomes a design output; some regions
may have to shrink or stabilize — flagged, not yet specified anywhere.

**Sub-decisions produced by running the balance sheet (same session):**

- **DEC-002.1 — Energy consumption target restated [ACCEPTED]:** the 4,000
  kWh/cap/yr floor is indefensible once manufacturing (800–1,800 kWh/cap/yr),
  water system (50–125), desalination (15–25), and own-food green ammonia (50–80)
  claims are subtracted. Restated: 4,000–6,000 applies to buildings+transport;
  total system target in industrialized regions is 5,000–6,000 kWh/cap/yr.
  (Energy log amendment.) Alternative preserved: DEFENDING the original 4,000
  floor would have required cutting manufacturing demand ~2× below its own branch's
  estimate — rejected on the materials log's own numbers.
- **DEC-002.2 — Conditional polymer feedstock cap [ACCEPTED, then superseded same
  session by DEC-003:** biomass feedstock only in water-abundant regions with
  confirmed ≥15% food-branch arable surplus]. Superseded the same day — see DEC-003.
- **DEC-002.3 — Labor claim passed forward [RECORDED]:** material provisioning
  = 13–19% of population (21–34% of working-age pool) — the node's largest fixed
  claim on the rest of society; Domains II/V must design around it. Not a choice —
  a computed finding, recorded here because it will bind every future domain.

**Propagations:** every future branch work package must compute its claims against
this sheet; unfilled cells (§3 of the sheet) are assigned owners (agronomic
modeling → food branch; per-material energy bill → materials branch; energy/water
labor → respective branches; ammonia population denominators → Domain III).

**Where logged:** 01-1-resource-balance-sheet.md (created); integration file
(Blocker 2 resolution); Energy log (DEC-002.1); Materials log (DEC-002.1,
DEC-002.2); Food log (land-budget dependency).

### DEC-003 — Biomass polymer feedstock sourcing vs. food land

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, Node I.1 integration session (Blocker 3).
**Scope:** [Raw Materials & Manufacturing] × [Food/Agriculture]; Contradiction C.

**Question:** How should the 20–30% biomass polymer pillar be sourced, and what
happens to the 15% arable-land cap?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-003-alt-A — Residue-first, arable cap drops from 15% to 5% [CHOSEN]:** the
  20–30% biomass share must be carried by residues and waste streams (straw, husk,
  bagasse, paper-stream cellulose) plus marginal-land perennials (miscanthus,
  switchgrass on degraded/idle land) — never dedicated arable crops. The arable cap
  falls to 5%, exception-only (legacy processing plants, transition years).
  Trade-off: residue supply is seasonal/dispersed, so polymer biorefineries must be
  smaller and regionalized (matches the RMA hub architecture anyway), and
  conversion yields are 20–30% lower than food-grade feedstock, raising cost —
  accepted in exchange for eliminating the food-polymers land conflict entirely.
- **DEC-003-alt-B — Keep 15% arable cap, add per-region land-audits before feedstock
  allocation [NOT CHOSEN]:** every water-abundant region wanting feedstock runs a
  joint food-materials land audit proving ≥15% surplus after climate-adapted
  crop-mix scenarios. Trade-off: auditing machinery vs. serial food-branch veto
  points that could starve the materials branch of feedstock certainty, undermining
  its investment case.
- **DEC-003-alt-C — Rebalance pillars: biomass falls to 10–15%, CO₂-derived rises to
  15–25% [NOT CHOSEN]:** swap a land-dependency for an energy-dependency (funded by
  the 5,000–6,000 kWh/cap/yr surplus and paired with electrolyzer infrastructure).
  Trade-off: CO₂-to-polymer at scale is less mature than biomass fermentation — a
  bet on an R&D trajectory; uncertain electrolysis economics.
- **DEC-003-alt-D — Demand reduction as primary pillar at 40–50%, biomass shrinks to
  10–15% [NOT CHOSEN]:** longer product lifetimes, the 5,000 SKU cap, repair rights,
  and design-for-disassembly cut polymer demand so deeply that only 10–15% biomass
  (residue-carried) is needed. Trade-off: demands a cultural/materiality shift
  Domain XI hasn't been consulted on, and underestimates non-discretionary polymer
  demand (packaging hygiene, medical, safety).

**Decision:** alt-A. Residue-first sourcing; 15% cap replaced outright with a 5%
exception-only cap; food-branch land-surplus certification no longer required.

**Rationale:** converts competing claims on the same irrigated/fertile arable
(equivalent to ~10–25 Mha globally) into complementary uses; dispersed residue
supply fits the RMA's regionalized hub architecture rather than fighting it.

**Trade-offs accepted:** smaller/more numerous biorefineries; 20–30% lower
conversion yields (higher cost). New coupling created: residue removal rates must
protect the food branch's 3% SOM floor (lignin/cellulose fractions returned to
fields) — owned by the food branch's residue-management design.

**Propagations:** Food log dependency updated (supersedes DEC-002.2's conditional
structure); integration file Contradiction C resolved; balance sheet §2.3/§4.2
marked superseded.

**Where logged:** Materials log (polymer feedstock strategy amended, status firm;
open tension RESOLVED; cross-domain dependency updated); Food log (land dependency
superseded); integration file (Contradiction C resolution); balance sheet
(supersession notes).

**Explorable branches:** alt-D reactivates if Domain XI consumption-culture work
endorses a strong materiality shift — it is *compatible* with alt-A's residue
sourcing and would simply shrink the required biomass share further. alt-C
reactivates if electrolyzer economics beat projections AND residue logistics prove
intractable. alt-B reactivates if residue yields disappoint regionally and
dedicated crops are re-examined (the audit machinery is the slow path to the same end).

### DEC-004 — Sectoral authority arbitration: problem specified, mechanism deferred

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, Node I.1 integration session (Blocker 4).
**Scope:** all four sectoral authorities (RFA/REA/RMA/WA); Domain III handoff;
new artifact 01-1-authority-arbitration-spec.md.

**Question:** How should the node handle the four-authority arbitration gap before
Domain III exists?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-004-alt-A — Document the conflict, defer mechanism to Domain III [CHOSEN]:**
  a formal problem-spec document (01-1-authority-arbitration-spec.md): four
  authorities, four boundary logics, mapped pairwise collision points with real
  examples, what each authority must be able to impose on the other, and
  requirements any Domain III meta-framework must satisfy. No arbitration mechanism
  designed here. Trade-off: keeps work packages honest and small, but leaves "who
  decides tonight" formally open — if Domain III stalls, the four authorities stay
  unaccountable to each other.
- **DEC-004-alt-B — Design a minimal inter-authority protocol now: joint siting
  boards per resource corridor [NOT CHOSEN]:** wherever two authorities' core
  mandates touch the same physical resource, a standing joint site board (2+2
  delegates plus one neutral) approves/resolves on the record, appealable to the
  future meta-framework. Trade-off: real arbitration muscle today, but pre-commits
  a governance structure Domain III hasn't shaped — risk that joint boards calcify
  into a fifth quasi-authority (the governance-monoculture drift the integration
  review flagged).
- **DEC-004-alt-C — Boundary-fix at the source: single physical-territory
  jurisdictions per region [NOT CHOSEN]:** collapse foodshed = energy region =
  manufacturing region = watershed into one region boundary, authorities as
  sectoral departments of one regional government. Trade-off: eliminates overlap by
  construction and honors "change the pond," but contradicts each branch's
  carefully-argued scale logic (hydrological determinism vs. agroecology vs. grid
  topology) — highest rework cost against four completed branches.
- **DEC-004-alt-D — Fixed priority hierarchy: water > food > energy > materials
  [NOT CHOSEN]:** a lexical ordering applied to all conflicts. Trade-off: crisp and
  computable, but hardcodes asymmetry without context-sensitivity and creates
  systematic blind spots (energy emergencies "win" that would have been better
  handled by coordinated rationing).

**Decision:** alt-A. Formal problem specification written; mechanism explicitly
deferred; Domain III owns the mechanism question, the node owns the problem.

**Rationale:** the integration file's Blocker-4 guidance required an explicit
deferral with a well-specified problem statement; alt-B would pre-commit governance
ahead of the meta-framework (monoculture risk), alt-C would reopen four completed
branches, alt-D is a mock solution.

**Contents of the spec (for the record):** §1 four authorities tabulated (boundary
logic, scale, inviolable mandate, exit mechanism — noting WA alone has no exit
mechanism); §2 seven collision points (drought Stage 3 vs. nuclear cooling; tiered
crop targets vs. hydrological allocation; mine consent vs. watershed protection;
peri-urban reserves vs. industry siting; ammonia dispatch vs. fertilizer floor;
industrial curtailment vs. production quotas; WA exit-mechanism gap); §3 six
requirements on any meta-framework (incl. dispute resolution faster than the
fastest physical trigger it governs; no unbonded unilateral bounding of another
authority's core mandate; consent binding across all relevant authorities
pre-vote); §4 three warnings (no apex arbiter; no fifth tripartite clone; no
silent WA exit-gap fill); §5 transition rule (interim inter-authority agreements
must be loggable against the §2 collision table); §6 stall fallback stated honestly.

**Trade-offs accepted:** cross-sector conflicts unresolvable until Domain III;
inter-authority "debt" accrues in the interim (documented, not hidden).

**Propagations:** Domain III handoff now demands an item-by-item response to the
spec; the branch logs of all four branches carry cross-references; no fifth
sectoral authority should be designed in other domains until Domain III answers §3.

**Where logged:** 01-1-authority-arbitration-spec.md (created); integration file
(Contradiction D resolution + Domain III handoff updated); all four branch logs
(tension sections cross-referenced).

### DEC-005 — Nuclear share under dry cooling in water-stressed regions

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, Node I.1 integration session (Blocker 5).
**Scope:** [Energy] × [Water & Sanitation]; Contradiction B.

**Question:** How should the nuclear share be handled in water-stressed arid
regions to break the dry-cooling efficiency feedback loop?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-005-alt-A — Regional nuclear cap tiered by water stress [CHOSEN]:** keep
  30–40% nuclear where water is adequate; in water-stressed regions
  (<1,700 m³/cap/yr, same Falkenmark tiers as food/water), nuclear is capped at
  20–25% and must use hybrid dry cooling (≤10% of wet-cooling water use), with the
  lost share replaced by extra solar+storage and the region's HVDC interconnects.
  Trade-off: arid regions carry more storage/import cost — ~0.1–0.3 cent/kWh
  premium, absorbed within the restated 5,000–6,000 kWh/cap/yr target (per DEC-002),
  not on top of it.
- **DEC-005-alt-B — Hold 30–40% everywhere, mandate hybrid cooling as the
  requirement [NOT CHOSEN]:** all new nuclear in water-stressed regions
  hybrid-cooled, sized so total water draw fits inside the WA agricultural
  residual. Trade-off: the feedback loop is damped, not broken — a 30–40% share
  under hybrid cooling still adds 2–4% parasitic drag on every nuclear MWh in arid
  regions; regions below ~1,000 m³/cap/yr may still hit hard infeasibility, and
  the spec doesn't say what happens then.
- **DEC-005-alt-C — Nuclear-optional in arid interiors: replace with geothermal or
  deep-storage where geography allows [NOT CHOSEN]:** if dry cooling makes nuclear
  marginal in deserts, don't fight it; substitute enhanced geothermal,
  long-duration storage, or heavy HVDC import dependence. Trade-off: makes the
  arid grid architecture geography-lottery-dependent — some arid regions have
  neither geothermal nor solar overbuild room, and no fallback class is specified.

**Decision:** alt-A. Nuclear share tiered by water stress; hybrid dry cooling
mandated in stressed regions; displaced share filled by solar+storage overbuild
and HVDC imports.

**Rationale:** breaks the loop by construction — the dry-cooling penalty (2–5%
efficiency + 1–2% parasitic fan load) stays below compounding scale when the share
is halved in exactly the regions where water binds; reuses the stress taxonomy
already adopted in DEC-001/002/003 (one classification across the node); mirrors
the existing "exceptional hydro may omit nuclear" precedent with an arid
counterpart.

**Trade-offs accepted:** higher storage/interconnect cost in arid regions;
nuclear's contested status retained (revisitable if storage improves dramatically);
arid regions sit at the 20–25% cap unless geothermal or HVDC endowments justify
going lower — recorded as a future judgment call, not silently decided.

**Propagations:** Energy log (nuclear decision amended); Water log (cooling
decision cross-ref; dry-cooling open tension RESOLVED); integration file
(Contradiction B resolution; Verdict revised to "Settled").

**Where logged:** Energy log, Water log, integration file, balance sheet
(§4.1 interplay noted).

**Explorable branches:** alt-C reactivates for regions with real geothermal
endowments (any future arid-region grid deep-dive should check geothermal potential
first — it would be a special case of alt-A, going below the 20–25% cap). alt-B
reactivates if hybrid-cooling costs fall far enough that the parasitic drag is
noise even at 30–40%; it also remains the *transition-period* physics for existing
plants grandfathered into the system.

### DEC-006 — Freight allocation mechanism: modal hierarchy vs. road pricing

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, node I.2 work package (branch I.2.1 Transport of
Goods, first of the accepted breadth-first sequencing: I.2.1 → I.2.2 → I.2.3 →
early Tier-2 over I.1+I.2 → Domain II).
**Scope:** [Resource & Material Base → Transport of Goods]; nodes I.1 (all four
branches) as inherited constraint set.

**Question:** How should freight be assigned to modes given the restated
4,000–6,000 kWh/cap/yr buildings+transport electricity band — by price signals
 alone, or by structure?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-006-alt-A — Licensed modal hierarchy with hard electrification priority
  [CHOSEN]:** fixed order rail (≥1 Mt/yr corridors) > waterborne >
  battery-electric road (catenary ≥2,000 t/day) > exception only (grounds:
  time <72 h, quality, geography). RTA publishes per-OD-pair hierarchy tables;
  graduated exception fees 0.5–2.0 ct/t-km; targets ≥60% t-km rail+water
  (industrialized) / ≥40% (arid); 5-year review. Trade-off: forfeits
  door-to-door flexibility; RTA licensing staff 40–80/region.
- **DEC-006-alt-B — Road-charging/kilometer pricing only [NOT CHOSEN]:**
  internalize externalities via the price, let carriers choose mode. Real-world
  record (Germany Maut since 2005 and similar European truck-toll systems)
  shows 0–2% modal shift over ~20 years — an order of magnitude short of the
  20–30% the energy arithmetic requires — and pricing cannot act on the
  electricity-budget coupling at all.
- **DEC-006-alt-C — Status-quo logistics: carriers optimize, electrification
  happens by fleet turnover [NOT CHOSEN]:** no hierarchy; road stays dominant;
  the 400–1,200 kWh/cap/yr land-transport band is breached at scale once
  manufacturing (800–1,800 kWh/cap/yr), water (50–125), desal (15–25), and
  own-food ammonia (50–80) claims are met. Rejected as arithmetically
  unavailable, not merely inferior.

**Decision:** alt-A. Rail-vs-road gap (~65–115 kWh/cap/yr on arid grain-band
freight alone; rail 0.03–0.05 vs road 0.7–1.0 kWh/t-km) is the binding lever —
mode structure, not price.

**Trade-offs accepted:** administrative overhead (RTA staff); reduced
door-to-door flexibility concentrated into drayage + exception windows.

**Propagations:** authority accumulation (RTA = 4th sectoral authority — enters
the arbitration spec's collision table, DEC-008); Domain II infrastructure
charges classification; node I.2 branches I.2.2/I.2.3 (storage siting and
allocation mechanism both inherit the hierarchy corridors).

**Where logged:** `01-2-1_transport-of-goods-log.md` (§1, firm with fee schedule
tentative); design full doc: `01-2-1_transport-of-goods-full.md` §1.

**Explorable branches:** alt-B reactivates if the hierarchy's administrative
cost proves heavier than the efficiency gap it buys, or as a complementary
pricing layer beneath the hierarchy (not instead of it) — condition: fee-shift

### DEC-010 — Storage classification: closed four-class system vs. qualitative "critical goods"

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, node I.2 work package (branch I.2.2 Storage &
Supply Chains, second of the breadth-first sequencing: I.2.1 done → I.2.2 →
I.2.3 → early Tier-2 over I.1+I.2 → Domain II).
**Scope:** [Storage & Supply Chains] — operationalizes DEC-009's buffer
decision (six-week critical-goods stock) by defining its classification.

**Question:** DEC-009 mandated a six-week buffer of "critical goods" but left
"critical" example-defined. How is the buffer class defined so it can't expand
into general social overhead?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-010-alt-A — Two-number test + four closed classes [CHOSEN]:** every
  stored good classified by failure impact and rescue window into Class B
  (buffer: impact >72 h AND rescue window short enough that buffer bridges it —
  6-wk stock, RTA custody, rotation audit), Class F (flow: 2–5-day perishables,
  cold chain — resilience via redundant flow, not stock), Class S (specialist:
  branch-owned mandated stockpiles — energy's 2-yr nuclear fuel/10% spare
  transformers, materials' 6–18-month minerals — this branch provides custody
  only), Class C (ordinary, the default). Class B is closed: additions need a
  logged two-number classification decision with consigning-branch blocking
  minority; goods missing from the register default to Class C.
- **DEC-010-alt-B — Qualitative "critical" determined by each consigning branch
  [NOT CHOSEN]:** each branch declares its own criticals. Rejected: the buffer
  expands by lobbying until the 6-week capital trap becomes general overhead —
  exactly the quiet scope creep the project's decay analysis predicts; no
  objective gate exists.
- **DEC-010-alt-C — No classes: uniform buffer mandate on all inter-regional
  goods [NOT CHOSEN]:** rejected arithmetically — uniform 6-week cover on all
  flows is ~11.5% of total system inventory held idle (6/52), several times the
  node-buffer cost (27–32 kt per 2M-pop node vs. easily 3–5× that under a
  uniform mandate), for protection most flows don't need.

**Decision:** alt-A. Node buffer arithmetic (2M-person region): grain
25–29 kt, ammonia 1.2–1.8 kt, treatment chemicals 0.2–0.4 kt, medicines
0.1–0.4 kt — total 27–32 kt, ~15–40 M USD of node warehouse structure, plus
~6–14 kWh/cap/yr cold-chain electricity inside the buildings+transport band.

**Trade-offs accepted:** closure excludes goods whose true rescue window is
longer than any buffer (supply must be redesigned, not stocked — seed stock
goes to Class S-food, agronomy-sized); per-good thresholds stay tentative to
give the register room without reopening the class.

**Propagations:** DEC-009's buffer is now operational (classification,
custody, ledger, rotation); classification register is a new cross-publishing
surface under arbitration-spec §3 requirement 3; no new authority — storage
governance splits RTA (custody, ledger, facilities) / consigning branches
(quantities, drawdown).

**Where logged:** `01-2-2_storage-supply-chains-log.md` (§1, decision 1, firm
with per-good thresholds tentative); full doc §1.

**Explorable branches:** alt-B reactivates if the register shows real goods
repeatedly refused Class B that then fail in interruption events — evidence
the two-number test is mistuned, fixable at the 5-year review without
reopening the closure rule itself.

### DEC-012 — Dual-origin rule for the grain band and other monoflows

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, node I.2 work package (branch I.2.2).
**Scope:** [Storage & Supply Chains] × [Food/Agriculture] (DEC-001 grain band)
× [Raw Materials & Manufacturing] (source-diversity-floor precedent).

**Question:** Does the grain band — a designed, firm-delivery dependency —
carry a supplier-diversity requirement like the materials log's, and at what
threshold?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-012-alt-A — Dual-origin, no origin >60% [CHOSEN]:** any inter-regional
  flow covering >25% of a staple's calories needs ≥2 qualified origins, max
  60% from one; origin qualification = joint RFA (foodshed certification) +
  RTA (corridor credential); register records origins, % split, booked slots,
  buffer coverage; applies by analogy to ammonia, treatment chemicals,
  medicines. Failure arithmetic: at 125 kg/cap/yr, one origin failing at 60%
  puts 75 kg/cap/yr at risk; the 6-week buffer covers ~12 kg/cap, so recovery
  requires volume migration to the secondary origin within the ~4–8-week
  harvest-transition window — hence the 60/40 split must be real, not token.
- **DEC-012-alt-B — Materials-style 40% floor applied unchanged [NOT CHOSEN]:**
  stricter, more resilient… but grain origins are numerous and substitutable
  where mineral processing capacity is not; a 40% cap on band origins would
  force each arid region to maintain ~3 qualified supply relationships at
  band-sustaining scale, overshooting what the eligible wet-region pool can
  certify.
- **DEC-012-alt-C — No diversity rule: firm delivery obligations suffice
  [NOT CHOSEN]:** rejected — an obligation one origin alone can meet is a
  single-point famine failure (2010 Russian export ban class: a wheat export
  halt propagating through single-corridor import dependencies).

**Decision:** alt-A. The 60% threshold is a deliberate, named relaxation of the
materials log's 40% supplier floor for substitutable origins.

**Trade-offs accepted:** dual-origin qualification constrains the band to
origins with spare caloric capacity — a real cost passed to Domain II's band
design; token secondary suppliers prohibited (split must be real).

**Propagations:** Domain II (band instruments become bilateral long-term
contracts with origin-split terms, not commodity trade); RFA gains origin
qualification duty; the classification register carries per-flow origin-split
records; buffer sizing (DEC-009/DEC-010) confirmed as logistics-failure cover,
not harvest-failure cover.

**Where logged:** `01-2-2_storage-supply-chains-log.md` (§1, decision 3, firm
with threshold/process tentative, Domain II owning treaty mechanics); full
doc §3.

**Explorable branches:** alt-B reactivates if band-origin concentration
events recur despite the 60/40 rule (evidence the relaxation was too loose);
alt-C reactivates only if Domain III's arbitration mechanism proves able to
enforce firm delivery obligations against origins faster than failures
propagate — the rule sunsets only when enforcement is proven, not before.

### DEC-014 — Priority classes for curtailable scarce inputs

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, node I.2 work package (branch I.2.3 Allocation
Mechanisms, third and last branch of node I.2 before the early Tier-2
integration over I.1+I.2).
**Scope:** [Allocation Mechanisms] × [Transport] × [Energy] × [Materials];
generalizes the arbitration spec's §2.8/§2.9 protected floors.

**Question:** When a scarce input must be curtailed, who is protected and in
what order — pre-agreed classes or case-by-case boards?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-014-alt-A — Four published priority classes [CHOSEN]:** P1
  life-support (hospitals, water treatment, sanitation — never below
  lifeline) > P2 critical infrastructure ops (grid black-start/reserve,
  spine ops, firefighting, the protected ammonia floor from spec §2.5, buffer
  rotation) > P3 food-chain ops (harvest machinery, processing, cold chain,
  band origination/warehousing) > P4 everything else. Classes published with
  goods in the classification register; curtailment follows class order
  without discretionary reordering; within-class pro-rata by booked volume.
- **DEC-014-alt-B — Case-by-case emergency boards [NOT CHOSEN]:** each
  curtailment event adjudicated on merits. Rejected: case-by-case ranking
  under time pressure is the historical entry point for capture and
  favoritism — the water log removed discretionary drought triggers for
  exactly this class of failure; also violates arbitration-spec requirement
  2 (resolution faster than the fastest physical trigger) since boards decide
  in committee cycles, not hours.
- **DEC-014-alt-C — Market-curtailed by ability to pay [NOT CHOSEN]:**
  rejected — price-based curtailment allocates by willingness-to-pay,
  concentrating breakdown pressure on the least able to bear it; breaks the
  no-market lineage at the point where it matters most (life-supporting
  scarcity).

**Decision:** alt-A. Real-world basis: the EU's 2022 gas demand-reduction
regulation (Council Regulation (EU) 2022/1854) protected-consumer classes —
worked because pre-agreed, not negotiated mid-crisis.

**Trade-offs accepted:** fixed classes are coarse — a genuinely
life-supporting P3 claim cannot leapfrog P2 without an exception event
(latency cost accepted; exception frequency goes to the RTA's annual audit).

**Propagations:** the arbitration spec's §2.8 (agro-machinery) and §2.9
(ammonia slot pair) requirements become instances of the general scale;
energy lifeline rate and water Stage-3 caps become P1 content; Domain III
must confirm class ordering against any arbitration design it builds.

firm); full doc §1.

then the ladder is revised at the 5-year review, not bypassed ad hoc.

**Question:** The R-ladder's age-based triggers (R1 >2 wk; R2 >4 wk; R3
>8 wk) scheduled the full-emergency stage R3 two weeks after the
buffer's full-stretch exhaustion (~wk 5.65–6.03, verified by recompute);
R3's stated sustenance premise ("buffer at full stretch") was therefore
arithmetically false exactly at the ladder's failure mode. How is the ladder
re-cut?

### DEC-021 — Scarcity-ladder crosswalk: ownership, governing rule, e-fuel class (I.2.3 fix, resolves Contradiction C)

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, node I.2 integration-fix session (resolution
item 3 of the `01-2-integration.md` prioritized list).

**Question:** The node holds three published scarcity-ordering schemes with
no crosswalk governing co-occurring scarcity — the water log's allocation
hierarchy + staged drought protocol (env. flows > domestic > essential >
ag > industrial > non-essential; Stage 3 cap 150 L/p/d, Stage 4 50 L/p/d),
Allocation Decision 1's P1–P4 priority classes (life-support > critical
infrastructure > food-chain > everything else), and transport Decision 3's
e-fuel order (aviation first, shipping second, surplus to ag machinery) —
and the register carries no e-fuel priority class. Overlapping claimants
sit at different heights on different ladders (agriculture below domestic
on water but P3 on inputs; industrial P4 on goods but above non-essential
on water). Who owns the crosswalk, which ladder governs co-occurring
scarcity, and what class do e-fuels carry?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **Round 1 — where the crosswalk lives:**
  - **DEC-021-alt-A (ownership) — Allocation branch owns it; the register
    is the host file [CHOSEN]:** the register is already the node's "one
    canonical place per good, two numbers" artifact and the I.2 review
    names the register design as the home; the crosswalk becomes a new
    decision in `01-2-3_allocation-mechanisms-full.md` (amendment to
    Decision 1's register mechanism), water and transport logs each get a
    one-line cross-reference. Cost: allocation absorbs a table whose
    custody sits across three branches — more cross-domain bookkeeping
    there.
  - **DEC-021-alt-B (ownership) — Water branch owns it [NOT CHOSEN]:**
    the drought ladder is the most physically urgent (triggers fire on
    real storage), so the water log hosts and allocation defers. Rejected:
    breaks the register's "carries the priority column" architecture —
    the scarcity crosswalk would live outside the file whose design
    decision defines the register, splitting the priority system across
    two owning files.
  - **DEC-021-alt-C (ownership) — The arbitration spec hosts it as a new
    authority-collision row set [NOT CHOSEN]:** rejected — the spec is a
    problem-input document for Domain III, not an operative register;
    putting a live lookup table in it changes the spec's role, and the
    review did not ask for that.
- **Round 2 — the governing rule when two ladders disagree:**
  - **DEC-021-alt-A (rule) — Per-resource precedence [CHOSEN]:** each
    ladder governs only its own resource; water curtailment follows the
    water ladder, input curtailment follows the P-ladder, e-fuel follows
    its class rule; a claimant under simultaneous curtailment takes its
    own declared position on each ladder independently; **no supremacy
    clause**. The ag "contradiction" dissolves: criticized on water
    (below domestic — domestic is biologically fixed), protected on
    machinery fuel (P3 — harvest is time-critical); different questions,
    different answers. Cost: no combined floor for a claimant hit from
    both sides — the arbitration spec accepts a new deduction row
    (spec §2.11) rather than a number.
  - **DEC-021-alt-B (rule) — Best-position rule [NOT CHOSEN]:** a claimant
    curtailed on two resources takes the higher (more protective) of its
    ladder positions on both. Rejected: silently upgrades P4 industry and
    lowers the effective water cut for agriculture during Stage 3–4 —
    rewrites the water ladder's deliberately chosen sacrifice order
    without the water log saying so; re-litigates a firm decision by side
    door.
  - **DEC-021-alt-C (rule) — Water-stage supremacy [NOT CHOSEN]:** at
    drought Stage 3–4 the water stage governs input curtailment too.
    Rejected: honest about water being the binding constraint in arid
    regions, but makes the P-ladder stage-dependent — the register's "two
    numbers per good" stops being constant, and every register consumer
    (storage protocol template, ration-ladder triggers) must learn a
    third column; grows the design the crosswalk was meant to shrink.
- **Round 3 — what class e-fuel gets in the register:**
  - **DEC-021-alt-A (class) — Class follows the mission propelled
    [CHOSEN]:** register e-fuel not as one row but as a rule — an e-fuel
    allocation takes the priority class of the mission it propels
    (machinery P3; a ship carrying grain-band freight takes the cargo's
    class; discretionary aviation P4). Transport Decision 3's
    aviation-first reservation stands on the production-scheduling side
    only — a schedule guarantee, not an immunity; under curtailment,
    P-class order governs who keeps fuel, published air→ship→machinery
    order becomes the within-class tie-break. Cost: a passenger-flight
    cut in a Stage-3 drought becomes possible, which transport Decision 3
    never had to state.
  - **DEC-021-alt-B (class) — E-fuel ladder survives as its own column
    [NOT CHOSEN]:** air→ship→machinery kept inside the register as a
    class-independent priority that outranks P-classes for e-fuel.
    Rejected: a fourth standing ladder — exactly the parallel-scheme
    pattern Contradiction C condemns — and would protect discretionary
    flying above harvest machinery during a real shortage.
  - **DEC-021-alt-C (class) — One class for all e-fuel (P3) [NOT
    CHOSEN]:** simplest register row; pro-rata by booked volume.
    Rejected: erases the published ordering entirely — machinery and
    discretionary aviation become equals, remote-region harvests compete
    with holiday flights at the same priority, and the transport branch's
    declining schedule loses both its reserve shape and its internal
    ordering.

**Decision:** all three alt-A's (A / 1 / A as presented in the
interview rounds). Recorded as DEC-021.1 (allocation owns, register
hosts), DEC-021.2 (per-resource precedence, no supremacy clause,
compound case → spec §2.11), DEC-021.3 (mission-propelled class).
Amended into `01-2-3_allocation-mechanisms-full.md` (Decision 1
amendment block + §1 AMENDED mirror entry + §2 residual), the Allocation
log (§1 AMENDED entry + §2 residual), the Water log and Transport log
(each a cross-ref entry + mirrored full-doc §3 line), and the arbitration
spec (§2.11 row added).

**Rationale:** one crosswalk plus per-resource precedence removes the
node's only un-governed co-occurrence without rewriting any ladder's
deliberate sacrifice order; the ag/industrial "contradiction" was two
correct answers to two different questions. Registering e-fuel by
mission-propelled class honors transport Decision 3's published order on
the supply side while closing the curtailment gap the register's
"one register, two numbers" promise left open. The water log deploys the
same inherit-verbatim pattern (storage Decision 4's protocol template);
hosting in the register keeps every scarcity lookup in one file.

**Trade-offs accepted:** no combined curtailment floor exists at node
level until Domain III builds the spec §2.11 deduction row (residual
logged in the allocation log §2); discretionary aviation loses
curtailment immunity in a Stage-3 drought (transport Decision 3's
reservation honestly re-scoped); register rows carry potentially three
declared positions per good (class, priority, per-ladder placements).

**Propagations:** arbitration spec §2.11 (added this session — WA ×
consigning authorities, simultaneous multi-resource curtailment of one
claimant, with related rows §2.1/§2.9 named); water log cross-ref (ladder
content unchanged and firm; placement-only change); transport log
cross-ref (published order unchanged on the scheduling side); register
definition (storage log Decision 1's "two numbers per good") gains the
crosswalk surface operationally without touching storage's class logic.
Contradiction C of `01-2-integration.md` resolved; resolution item 3
closed.

**Where logged:** `01-2-3_allocation-mechanisms-log.md` (§1 amended
entry; §2 residual); `01-2-3_allocation-mechanisms-full.md` (Decision 1
amendment + mirrored block); `01-1-4_water-sanitation-log.md` (cross-ref
entry); `01-1-4_water-sanitation-full.md` (§3 mirrored line);
`01-2-1_transport-of-goods-log.md` (cross-ref entry);
`01-2-1_transport-of-goods-full.md` (§3 mirrored line);
`01-1-authority-arbitration-spec.md` (§2.11).

**Explorable branches:** alt-B (ownership) reactivates if the register
proves operationally distant from drought operations (crosswalk stale
against real Stage 3–4 events at audit time). alt-C (rule: best-position)

### DEC-022 — RTA span review: two internal divisions + dual-key decay review (resolves I.2 integration §4 finding 1, resolution item 6)

**Date/Session:** 2026-10-11, node I.2 integration-fix session (resolution
item 6 of the `01-2-integration.md` prioritized list).

**Question:** The RTA now holds nine functions (track, catenary, licensing,
spine designation, buffer custody, classification register, storage ledger,
WMS, priority classes — plus ration administration added by I.2.3), each
branch's concentration flag having assessed only its own slice; the
integration review §4 finding 1 diagnoses the compounded institution as the
essay's concentrated-institution decay profile at its strongest, and rules
the node needs a deliberate RTA-span review (I.1's Blocker-2-equivalent)
or an intra-RTA division design. How is the nine-function concentration
resolved, given that the arbitration spec §5 binds the node against adding
a sixth sectoral authority until Domain III answers?

**Choices presented (all preserved):**

- **DEC-022-alt-1 — Internal division, one authority, two governance
  tracks [CHOSEN]:** the RTA stays one legal body with an internal
  architecture — an Infrastructure Division (track, catenary, licensing,
  designation, warehouse shells) and a Logistics & Scarcity Division
  (register, storage ledger, WMS, priority classes, buffer custody
  operations, ration administration), each with its own published mandate,
  sub-board, and audit chain, top officers barred from both boards, audits
  run separately so each can catch the other; the scarcity division gets
  the stronger safeguards (civil-claims interfaces, published KPIs, the
  Domain IV confirmations already pending). Cost: architecture on paper
  until an auditor is alarmed — the discipline must be a standing review,
  not a one-time fix. Basis: the nine functions fall into two families
  that age differently — capital-deferral decay (visible, slow) vs.
  paper-flow favoritism decay (invisible, fast, the wartime-ration-board
  profile the allocation log already named).
- **DEC-022-alt-2 — Keep the RTA whole; standing published span audit
  instead [NOT CHOSEN]:** one annual RTA-span report enumerating every
  function, its decay indicator, and mitigation state, reviewed by the
  tripartite board + consigning minority. Rejected: accepts permanent
  concentration and bets the essay's entire decay profile on audit
  efficacy — the same bet the water log rejected for discretionary
  triggers; a merged report also re-creates the blending the split was
  meant to defeat.
- **DEC-022-alt-3 — Decompose: separate regional Logistics Authority
  [NOT CHOSEN]:** strongest structural answer, but creates a sixth
  sectoral authority — violating the arbitration spec §5 binding
  commitment before Domain III has answered, adding RL×RTA collision
  rows, and duplicating the WMS machinery the design elsewhere defended
  against exactly that fork's cost.

- **Review-machinery round (within alt-1):**
  - **DEC-022-alt-2.1 — Dual-key publication with named decay-KPI sets per
    division [CHOSEN]:** each division publishes its own annual report
    under its own signature — Infrastructure: deferred-maintenance
    backlog, exception-fee vs. capital needs, spine free-volume;
    Scarcity: Class B register drift (entries/exits without a logged
    two-number test), ration-share vs. the <20% Class C target,
    points-abuse rate, ledger-vs-physical deltas. Tripwire: two
    consecutive-year KPI breach → adversarial audit conducted by the
    other division's auditors, results to the consigning-sector blocking
    minority, who may force reorganization votes. Same pre-numeric-trigger
    logic the node applies to resources, pointed at the institution;
    arithmetic, not judgment. Cost: real reporting burden; first-year KPI
    bands wrong by construction (tentative).
  - **DEC-022-alt-1.1 — One merged annual RTA-span report [NOT CHOSEN]:**
    single report, one signature. Rejected: a merged narrative is exactly
    the cross-division blending the split was meant to defeat — one
    editor decides what the combined "RTA state" story is.
  - **DEC-022-alt-3.1 — Adversarial-only, event-triggered audits, no
    routine publication [NOT CHOSEN]:** cheapest annually, structurally
    strong when it fires. Rejected: nothing fires until damage is
    visible, and the trigger is administered by the institution under
    review — the flaw the water log rejected for discretionary drought
    response.

- **Propagation round — how existing documents reflect the two divisions:**
  - **DEC-022-alt-A — Selective amendment [CHOSEN]:** amend the arbitration
    spec (division-follows-function note for §2.8–2.11 counterparties) and
    the three I.2 logs' concentration tensions (span review resolved with
    residual); other files' "RTA" references stay as-is; the ledger entry
    maps every function to its division. Basis: real weight lands where
    the RTA counterparty matters; a sweep risks corrupting ten files for
    cosmetics.
  - **DEC-022-alt-B — Full-document sweep [NOT CHOSEN]:** rejected —
    large, mostly cosmetic edit wave with real drift risk.
  - **DEC-022-alt-C — New standalone artifact (rta-division-map.md), point
    only [NOT CHOSEN]:** rejected — creates a second canonical map the
    existing documents don't trace; the ledger entry serves that purpose
    without a new file.

**Decision:** alt-1 (internal division) + alt-2.1 (dual-key KPI review) +
alt-A (selective amendment). Recorded as **DEC-022.1** (two divisions,
function map below), **DEC-022.2** (dual-key review machinery), and
**DEC-022.3** (selective-amendment propagation scope).

**Function-to-division map:** Infrastructure Division — track, catenary,
licensing/exception fees, spine designation, warehouse shells. Logistics &
Scarcity Division — classification register, storage ledger, WMS,
priority classes, buffer custody operations, ration administration.

**Trade-offs accepted:** no new authority, but the split is paper until
operated — standing review is the load-bearing discipline; first-year KPI
bands wrong by construction (tentative, annual calibration); RTA remains
the single legal counterparty in all collision rows (division attribution
is internal, visible to auditors and Domain III, not a new jurisdiction).

**Propagations:** arbitration spec gains a division-follows-function note
above §2; transport log §1 AMENDED entry + §2 concentration tension
updated (+ full-doc mirror block); storage log and allocation log §2
RESOLVED entries (+ full-doc mirror blocks); the dual-key report's
Scarcity KPIs become the review surface for DEC-014's class drift, DEC-016's
20% ration-share target, and DEC-017's administration — targets that had
no review machinery; resolution item 6 closed; Domain III's read of the
RTA's institutional shape can now proceed.

**Where logged:** `01-2-1_transport-of-goods-log.md` (§1 amended entry; §2
updated); `01-2-1_transport-of-goods-full.md` (Decision 4 amendment +
§6 note + mirrored block); `01-2-2_storage-supply-chains-log.md` and
`01-2-3_allocation-mechanisms-log.md` (§2 RESOLVED entries + full-doc
mirrors); `01-1-authority-arbitration-spec.md` (internal-structure note).

**Explorable branches:** alt-2 (whole-RTA + span audit) reactivates if

# AGENTS.md — Society Redesign

Documentation-only repository for designing a rebuilt human society from first principles. There is no code, build, or test tooling. The work is a 12-domain structural map (`00_broad_structure.md`) tackled one branch at a time as "work packages." Outputs are markdown design proposals and running logs. The theoretical lens is the essay `02_AI-Essay.pdf`. Logged decisions are binding precedent.

## Repo state
- Git: branch `main`, remote `origin` = github.com/playa77/society. Commit messages name the work package and DEC range (e.g. "node I.2 branches … + ledger DEC-006..017").
- Absent: package manifests, Makefile, CI, tests, lockfiles, `.gitignore`. License: MIT.

## Build / test / lint
None exist. Do not invent commands (npm, make, pytest, etc.). Validate by hand with the checklist below.

## File map (classify by ownership before writing)
- `00_broad_structure.md` — the 12-domain map (I–XII) to level 3. Reference only.
- `01_project_context_prompt.md` — work-package prompt with a focus line filled in.
- `master_prompt_society_redesign.md` — reusable master prompt (focus placeholder); also holds the integration-session prompts. Not an interchangeable copy of 01.
- `02_AI-Essay.pdf` — vision essay ("You Don't Want It. Your Network Does."). Read with `pdftotext` or `read_file`.
- `03_running_log.md` — blank running-log template. Keep project content out of it.
